sn45.4:1.3: For Jānussoṇi, see [sn12.47:1.2]() and note. | A chariot drawn by mares was the preferred vehicle of Jānussoṇi ([mn99:30.1](), [mn27:2.1]()), as well as the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha [dn3:1.6.1](). Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.2.1 depicts Jānaśruti’s wealth as including cows, gold, and a chariot drawn by mules.
sn45.4:7.1: Another verse on Dhamma as a chariot is at [sn41.5:3.1](). | Chariots appear throughout the Vedic literature as vehicles of gods and heroes, and in metaphors especially for the sun and the sacrifice. Rig Veda 10.135.3 speaks of a chariot created by the mind, with a single pole and facing all directions, which connects a grieving son with his departed father.
sn45.4:8.3: It is not easy to differentiate the _dhura_ (“shaft”) from the _īsā_ (“pole”). The preceding line links the _dhura_ with the yoke, suggesting it is the shaft protruding from the body of the chariot, to which the yoke is connected crosswise for harnessing the beasts. Certain ancient images, such as the Indus Valley Daimabad toy chariot, clearly show a second part, a thicker pole with a cylindrical end into which the shaft was fitted. The metaphor starts with the beasts at the front and moves backwards, so I think the _īsā_ is this pole.
sn45.4:9.1: BB has “adornment” here, but parikkhara is always, so far as I know, used in the sense of something essential, as indeed is sila.
sn45.4:9.3: The Chinese parallel at SA 769 is exact and helpful: 捨三昧為轅.
